abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Medicines used in the treatment of viral infections usually reduce symptoms. There is a need to develop drugs that inhibit the viruses and do not merely relieve the symptoms. Natural bee products possess many pharmacological properties and are widely used in folk medicine. There are many studies on the antibacterial effects of bee products but little is known about their antiviral effects. An extensive literature search was conducted to find and summarize all articles about the antiviral activity of bee products such as bee bread, bee pollen, bee venom, beeswax, honey, propolis, and royal jelly. Analysis of the results showed that these products significantly affect RNA and DNA viruses, which are responsible for respiratory and digestive diseases. The bee products described in the review decrease the half‐maximal inhibitory concentration (IC50) and the half‐maximal effective concentration (EC50); they also increase the selectivity index (SI) values in comparison with controls. The mechanism of the antiviral effect of these products varies widely depending on the type of product and the virus. Thus, more in vitro and in vivo studies should be performed to confirm the use of bee products as a safe and promising adjunctive treatment in antiviral therapy. © 2025 The Author(s). sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: The most recent data from the World Health Organization (WHO) suggest that 3.7 billion people under 50, which constitutes 67% of the global population has herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV‐1) infection. In the case of herpes simplex virus type 2 (HSV‐2), the same data indicate that 491 million people aged 15 to 49 years (13% of the global population) are infected. Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection is a major public health issue due to ongoing global transmission. World Health Organization data from 2023 show that about 630 000 people died from HIV‐related causes and about 1.3 million people acquired HIV. In the case of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID‐19), since December 2019, over 760 million cases and 6.9 million deaths were reported by the WHO. 1 Many viral infections, such as HSV, coronavirus (CoV), and HIV, are treatable but not curable (Table 1). The medicines that we can use currently only reduce symptoms but cannot cure the infections. 1 , 2 , 3 There is another issue with viral hepatitis. According to the WHO, 354 million people live with hepatitis B or C because, for most of them, testing and treatment remain beyond their reach. Hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection can be prevented by safe and effective vaccines or antiviral agents in the case of chronic disease. There is no vaccine to treat hepatitis C virus (HCV) but antiviral medicines can cure more than 95% of HCV‐infected people. 1

sec.p: Antiviral drug resistance is a major obstacle for scientists, medical professionals, and government agencies as it prevents effective antiviral therapies. Gene mutations are responsible for drug resistance to pathogens, which leads to viral drug‐resistant phenotypes 4 and their ability to cause pandemics. 5 In humans, viral species can have multiple mutations, which can result in interaction and the production of specific phenotypes. Another problem in antiviral therapies is the lack of vaccines and antiviral drugs (Table 1). Alternative methods of treating viral infections are thus needed. To solve the problem, scientists analyze interactions between causes of antiviral drug resistance and potential new drugs, especially natural medicinal products. 5

This review summarizes up‐to‐date research on bee products (bee bread, bee pollen, bee venom, beeswax, honey, propolis, and royal jelly) used in different viral infection treatments, focusing only on in vitro assays.

sec.title: CHARACTERISTICS OF VIRUSES SENSITIVE TO BEE PRODUCTS
Double‐stranded DNA viruses
sec.p: Figure 1 provides information about double‐stranded DNA viruses. Adenoviruses (AdV) cause upper or lower respiratory tract, gastrointestinal tract, or conjunctiva infections in children and adults. 6 Herpes simplex viruses (HSV‐1 and HSV‐2) are α‐herpesviruses. Herpes simplex virus type 1 causes blister formation and inflammation of oral and ocular cells but sometimes the infection can lead to blindness, hearing impairment, and fatal encephalitis. Herpes simplex virus type 2 causes genital lesions. 21 Human papillomaviruses (HPV) cause warts or different types of cancer. 7 Lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV) is a cattle virus that can infect humans. Direct person‐to‐person transmission of this virus is also possible. 22 , 23 Infection with LSDV ‘can affect the respiratory tracts, digestive system, genitalia, and lymph nodes’. 22 , 23 Parapoxviruses infect sheep, goats, and humans (after contact with those animals) 24 and cause acute pustular skin lesions. 24 , 25 Varicella zoster virus (VZV) infects only humans without an animal reservoir; it causes varicella (also known as chickenpox) and zoster (also known as shingles). The primary infection of VZV is varicella or chickenpox in young children, which is characterized by fever, rash on the skin, and sometimes mucosa. Usually, it ceases in most patients within 2 weeks. After primary infection, VZV becomes latent in ganglionic neurons and reactivates as herpes zoster in the elderly and immunocompromised individuals. 26 , 27

sec.title: RNA viruses
sec.p: Figure 2 provides information about RNA viruses. Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is enveloped in plus‐strand RNA, a mosquito‐borne alphavirus, which causes inflammatory musculoskeletal disease in humans. The infection is ‘characterized by an abrupt onset of fever, frequently associated with joint pain’. 11 Coronaviruses (CoV) are positive‐sense, single‐stranded RNA viruses that cause respiratory diseases. HCoV‐229E, HCoV‐OC43, HCoV‐NL63, and HKU1 cause a mild upper respiratory disease and severe infections are rare, whereas SARS‐CoV infects the lower respiratory tract. 28

Enteroviruses (EV) and Group B of Coxsackievirus (CVB 1–6) are non‐enveloped, positive sense, single‐stranded RNA viruses. 29 , 30 Until now, more than 100 types of EV have been classified into four groups based on their molecular and biological characteristics: enterovirus A (EV‐A), enterovirus B (EV‐B), enterovirus C (EV‐C), and enterovirus D (EV‐D). Coxsackievirus B belongs to the EV‐B group. 30 Infections with EV can be asymptomatic or may cause ‘symptoms such as common cold, hand foot and mouth disease, aseptic meningitis, acute myocarditis, pericarditis, hepatitis, and encephalitis’. 29

The HCV is a single‐stranded RNA virus causing liver diseases such as fibrosis, cirrhosis, and eventually carcinoma of hepatic cells. 13 , 31 Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV‐1) is a positive‐strand RNA retrovirus causing the HIV/AIDS pandemic. 32 , 33 Influenza A viruses (IAV) are negative‐sense, single‐stranded RNA viruses. 34 So far, 18 HA and 11 NA subtypes have been identified. Influenza A viruses can infect aquatic birds, domestic animals, and humans. 35 Based on the virulence of IAV in chickens, the viruses are divided into two phenotypes: low pathogenic avian influenza (LPAI) and highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI). H4, H6, and H9 belong to LPAI, whereas H5 and H7 are classified as HPAI. 34 , 35

Mammalian orthoreovirus (reovirus) is a double‐stranded RNA (dsRNA) virus. 36 Reovirus infects humans. The infection is restricted to very young people and the virus causes from minimal to no symptoms. Reovirus can be useful as a cancer therapy because it can replicate in transformed cells of tumors, kill cancer cells, and augment anti‐tumor immunity. 36 , 37

Mayaro virus (MAYV) is a single‐stranded RNA virus, which causes Mayaro fever (characterized by long‐lasting arthralgia). 38 The Newcastle disease virus (NDV) is a negative‐sense, single‐stranded, non‐fragmented RNA virus 39 causing mild flu‐like symptoms or conjunctivitis and/or laryngitis in humans. 39 , 40 Noroviruses are non‐enveloped, single‐stranded RNA viruses 15 which cause gastroenteritis. Seven groups of noroviruses are known: GI to GVII. Only GI, GII, and GIV infect humans. 41 Polioviruses are non‐enveloped positive‐strand RNA viruses and human enteroviruses. 42 Poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) can invade the nervous system and cause paralysis. 4

Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) is an enveloped, non‐segmented, negative‐sense, single‐stranded RNA genome virus. Symptoms of infection include bronchiolitis and pneumonia in infants and young children, common colds in adults, and more serious respiratory illnesses in elderly or immunocompromised patients. 19 , 20 Rhinoviruses (RV) are single‐stranded, positive‐sense RNA viruses without an envelope causing severe respiratory illnesses (usually common colds). 43 Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV) is a Phlebovirus transmitted by mosquitoes and causes severe diseases in humans and ruminants. 44 In humans, RVFV may cause generalized fatigue, headache, low‐grade fever, joint pains, and photophobia. Infection can also lead to clinical manifestations, which, in severe cases, cause retinopathy, encephalitis, or disseminated intravascular coagulation, leading to hemorrhage. This virus is endemic throughout most of Africa; nevertheless, dissemination into Europe may occur. 45

Rubella virus (RUBV) is an airborne human pathogen that generally causes mild measles‐like symptoms, including fever and rash. It is a teratogen because the infection of a pregnant woman within the first trimester can result in miscarriage or congenital rubella syndrome (CRS). The latter is characterized by systemic inflammation of a neonate, inadequate organ development and intellectual disability, deafness, cardiac abnormalities, and developmental delays. 46 , 47

Rotaviruses (RoVs) infect a wide array of mammalian and avian hosts. There are more than eight genetically divergent species of RVs, although most human diseases are caused by group A strains. 48 Simian SA11, which belongs to this group, is the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis in young children. SA11 infects enterocytes, leading to malabsorption and diarrhea, which are stimulated by RV enterotoxin NSP4. 49 , 50 Vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV) is an enveloped, single‐stranded, negative‐sense RNA virus that infects various mammalian (cattle, horses, and swine) and insect cells. Infections in humans result in a mild febrile illness or can be asymptomatic. Symptoms of infection include vesicular lesions in the tongue, oro‐nasal mucosa, gums, teats, and coronary bands. 51 , 52

sec.title: MATERIALS AND METHODS
sec.p: In September 2023, PubMed and Google Scholar were searched for English‐language papers containing the following terms: (antiviral) AND (virus) AND (bee products) AND (propolis) OR (honey) OR (bee venom) OR (royal jelly) OR (bee pollen) OR (bee bread) OR (wax). This resulted in 1110 records being found on Google Scholar and 2250 on PubMed. Patents, clinical trials, theses, and book chapters were not taken into consideration. After the preliminary analysis based on the abstracts, 203 papers from Google Scholar and 140 from PubMed were selected for further investigation. Then, we analyzed 51 papers from Google Scholar and 42 papers from PubMed employing the exclusion and inclusion criteria. Exclusion criteria were: (i) inaccessible articles, (ii) languages other than English, (iii) review articles, (iv) absence of in vitro antiviral assays of bee products, (v) studies on animal viruses not pathogenic to humans, and (vi) assays involving geopropolis or mixtures of bee products with other compounds. Inclusion criteria were: (i) peer‐reviewed English‐language publications reporting antiviral in vitro and/or in vivo assays, (ii) studies analyzing ingredients isolated directly from bee products, and (iii) investigations involving viruses capable of causing disease in humans. Finally, the selected articles were divided into six groups based on the type of the tested bee product: there were 30 papers about propolis, one about royal jelly, nine about honey, five about bee bread and bee pollen, five about bee venom, and one about beeswax. Fifty one articles published between 1992 and 2023 were analyzed.

sec.title: ANTIVIRAL ACTIVITY OF BEE PRODUCTS
sec.p: Bee products such as bee bread, bee pollen, bee venom, beeswax, honey, propolis, and royal jelly possess antiviral activity, possibly because they are efficient virucidals: they enhance antiviral efficacy, stimulate immune response, block virus entry, and inhibit viral replication. 53 , 54 Unfortunately, the complete mechanism of bee products' antiviral activity is still unknown.

sec.title: Bee bread and bee pollen
sec.p: Bee pollen is a plant pollen collected by honey bees, and is used by bees to produce bee bread during a complex fermentation process performed by lactic acid bacteria and yeasts. 55 The process increases the bioavailability of pollen nutrients. Bee bread is composed of proteins, lipids, carbohydrates, flavonoids, phenolic compounds, fatty acids, free amino acids, enzymes, vitamins, macronutrients and micronutrients (Ca, P, Na, Mg, Mn, Fe, Cu, K, S, and Al). 53 , 56 Bee pollen is composed of proteins (5% to 60%), essential amino acids, sugars (13% to 55%), lipids (4% to 7%), nucleic acids, crude fiber (0.3% to 20%), minerals (Ca, Mg, Fe, Zn, Cu, K, and Na), vitamins (A, B1, B2, B3, B6, B7, B9, C, and E), enzymes, phytosterols (β‐sitosterol, P‐sitosterol, and terpenes), flavonoids (kaempferol, quercetin, isoquercitrin, isorhamnetin, and myricetin), and organic carotenoid pigments (lycopene and zeaxanthin). 53 , 54 The antiviral activity of bee pollen is related to flavonoids, especially quercetin, kaempferol and its derivatives, 54 and luteolin. 53 Bee pollen is relatively safe and has no side effects, 57 although it may cause allergic reactions or may contain trace amounts of contaminants (heavy metals or mycotoxins). 58

Didaras et al. 59 investigated the antiviral activity of Greek bee bread against enterovirus EV‐D68, cultured in human rhabdomyosarcoma cells. Eighteen bee bread samples, derived from various plant pollens and collected from different regions of Greece, were analyzed. The most effective samples were multifloral bee bread from Larissa, Heraklion, and Kozani, and citrus bee bread from Larissa. In contrast, multifloral bee bread from Arta and castanea bee bread from Mount Athos were less effective. Bee bread was shown to reduce the number of EV‐D68 copies. Table 2 presents the IC50 and selectivity index (SI) values. Three samples were only effective at cytotoxic concentrations, and the remaining 15 exhibited antiviral activity at non‐toxic levels. Notably, seven of the 15 active samples were effective at concentrations approximately 20 times lower than the CC50 for the cells. 59

sec.p: In 2023, Dimitriou et al. 60 measured the antiviral effect of Greek bee bread on the influenza A virus H1N1. The authors analyzed seven samples of bee bread as well as proteinaceous, n‐butanol, and aqueous bee bread fractions: 1‐BB, 4‐BB, 1‐BB‐P, 4‐BB‐P, 1‐BB‐Bu, 4‐BB‐Bu, 1‐BB‐H, 4‐BB‐H. Table 2 presents the IC50 and SI values that were obtained. In four samples, the SI values were higher than 20, suggesting a potent antiviral effect – the SI value indicates that ‘the IC50 concentration is more than 20 times lower than the correspondent CC50 concentration’. 60

The antiviral effects of bee pollen against Newcastle disease virus (NDV), influenza viruses, and enterovirus were analyzed by Babaei et al. 61 Didaras et al. 59 and Dimitriou et al. 60 Babaei et al. 61 evaluated the antiviral effect of pollen powder (1000 and 5000 mg kg−1) and virginiamycin (150 mg kg−1) against Newcastle disease virus (NDV). The authors observed insignificant changes in NDV antibody titrations for virginiamycin as well as 1.1‐ and 1.7‐fold increases for pollen powder in the doses of 1000 and 5000 mg kg−1. When compared with virginamycin, pollen powder therefore increased antibody titrations against Newcastle disease virus. 61

Besides studying bee bread, Dimitriou et al. 60 also measured the antiviral effect of Greek bee pollen against influenza A virus H1N1. The authors examined seven samples of fermented and bee‐collected pollen as well as proteinaceous, n‐butanol, and aqueous bee bread fractions AF1, AF‐4, AF‐5, AF‐17, AF1‐P, AF‐4‐P, AF‐5‐P, AF‐17‐P, 6P‐BCP, 6P‐BCP‐P, 6P‐BCP‐Bu, 6P‐BCP‐H. Table 2 presents the IC50 and SI values that were obtained. For bee pollen, the SI values in four samples were higher than 20, suggesting a potent antiviral effect. 60 Babaei et al. 61 also evaluated the antiviral effect of pollen powder (1000 and 5000 mg kg−1) and virginiamycin (150 mg kg−1) against avian influenza H9N2 viruses in Japanese quails. The authors observed an increase in antibody titrations: a twofold increase for virginiamycin, 1.6‐ and 2.2‐fold increases for pollen powder (1000 and 5000 mg kg−1). Consequently, when compared to virginamycin, pollen powder increased antibody titrations against Newcastle and avian influenza H9N2 viruses. 61

Besides the research on bee bread, Didaras et al. 59 analyzed the antiviral effect of Greek bee pollen on enterovirus D68. The authors analyzed two samples of bee pollen from different regions of Greece. Table 2 shows the IC50 values obtained for hedera (Mount Pelion) and multifloral (Thessaly) bee pollen, suggesting that bee pollen reduces the number of EV‐D68 copies. The SI values, also shown in Table 2, indicate that viral inhibition occurs in concentrations that are not toxic to the cells. 59

sec.title: Bee venom
sec.p: Bee venom is composed of water (> 80%), enzymes (phospholipase A2 and hyaluronidase), peptides (melittin, apamin, mast cell degranulating peptide, and adolapin), amino acids, phospholipids, sugars, biogenic amines, and pheromones. 54 The pH value of bee venom is between 4.5 and 5.5. 53 Interestingly, the antiviral effect of bee venom may be related to its anti‐inflammatory activity. 54 The antiviral effect may also be caused by melittin, which activates the immune system, and phospholipase A2, which prevents viral fusion with cells and replication. 53 Bee venom may also cause allergic and anaphylactic reactions. The main allergens are phospholipase A2, melittin, and hyaluronidase. Bee venom at a concentration of 100 μg mL−1 can cause limb paralysis, pain, dyspnea, nausea, unconsciousness, and lymphocyte instability, and a dose range from 2.8 to 3.5 mg of bee venom per kg of the human body can be lethal for allergic people. 62

Fenard et al. 63 analyzed the antiviral effect of p3bv peptide isolated from bee venom against human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), X4 HIV‐1 virus (HIV‐1BRU and HIV‐1HXB2), and R5 HIV‐1 (HIV‐1ADA and HIV‐1YU2). The p3bv peptide inhibits HIV‐1BRU replication but does not inhibit replication of HIV‐1ADA. The ID50 value of HIV‐1BRU and HIV‐1HXB2 replication was about 2 μM, whereas p3bv in concentrations higher than 10 μM fully inhibited viral replication. Interestingly, p3bv has no impact on HIV‐1ADA and HIV‐1YU2 replication. Moreover, p3bv (2 μM) hinders the cell to cell fusion between P4 cells and 293 cells which express a viral envelopeprotein from an X4 virus (HIV‐1HXB2). The authors also noticed that p3bv interacts with the major chemokine co‐receptor 4 (CXCR4) to inhibit X4 HIV‐1 strains. 63

Hassan et al. 64 measured the antiviral effect of bee venom against human adenovirus serotype 7 (Adeno‐7) and Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV). Both viruses were cultured in Vero cells. The IC50 value obtained is shown in Table 2. The results suggest that bee venom possesses antiviral activity towards DNA (Adeno‐7) and RNA (RVFV) viruses. The analysis of ethanol white wax extract showed an increase in infectivity titer post‐treatment of Adeno‐7 (1.66 log10 mL−1) and RVFV (0.65 log10 mL−1). In the case of post‐interferon treatment (5 ng mL−1), a decrease in the virus infectivity titer was 1.0 log10 mL−1 for RVFV. 64

Kim et al. 65 evaluated the antiviral activity of bee venom against human papilloma virus (HPV). The assay was performed using HPV‐infected CaSki and HeLa cells. The analysis of CaSki and HeLa showed that 24 h of bee venom (5 and 10 μg mL−1) treatment decreased HPV16 E6 and E7 mRNA expression. The authors observed 0.90±0.01‐ and 0.77±0.01‐fold decrease after 12 h in 5 μg ml−1 bee venom‐treated CaSki cells and 0.91±0.01 and 0.59±0.01‐fold one after 24 h in 5 μg ml−1 bee venom‐treated CaSki cells. The mRNA expression of HPV18 E6 in HeLa decreased at 24 h after 10 μg mL−1 bee venom treatment but the expression of HPV18 E7 was not altered. 65

Uddin et al. 66 measured the antiviral effect of bee venom against the influenza A virus (H1N1), vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV), respiratory syncytial virus (RSV), herpes simplex virus (HSV), enterovirus‐71 (EV‐71) and Coxsackie virus (H3). The VSV and HSV were cultured in Vero cells, EV‐71 and Coxsackie virus in HeLa cells, RSV in HEp‐2 cells, and H1N1 was cultured in allantoic fluid of 10‐day‐old chicken embryos. Table 2 shows the EC50 and SI values that were obtained. The authors also observed that 12 h pre‐treatment of the cells with bee venom (3 μg mL−1) reduced viral replication significantly at 24 h post‐infection (hpi) (354‐fold). Co‐incubation with bee venom (2.0 μg mL−1) at 4 °C for 30 min prior to cell inoculation reduced the viral titers at 24 hpi, compared to the untreated virus‐infected controls, by 175‐fold for H1N1, sevenfold for RSV, and ninefold for HSV. Co‐incubation with bee venom (2.0 μg mL−1) at 4 °C for 30 min before inoculating the cells caused an approximately 977‐fold decrease in viral titer of H3. In the case of EV‐71 infected cells, the TCID50 value was significantly higher than that in bee‐venom‐treated cells (a 131‐fold increase). 66

Sarhan et al. 67 measured the antiviral effect of Egyptian bee venom on the HCV. This virus was cultured in human hepatoma‐derived (Huh7it‐1) cells. The IC50 and CC50 values obtained were 0.05 and 20 000 ng mL−1, respectively, and the SI value was 400 000 (Table 2). The authors also observed that bee venom decreased HCV activity significantly and dose‐dependently. The analysis of HCV infectivity showed that pre‐treatment of cells and viruses for 2 h by bee venom (100 ng mL−1) significantly decreased HCV infectious particles, which suggests that the virucidal activity of bee venom is direct. HCV infectivity was decreased by bee venom (100 ng mL−1) in culture supernatants during post‐inoculation, suggesting inhibition of HCV replication within the cells or hindering HCV infectivity in culture supernatants. The analysis of HCV RNA level showed no impact of post‐inoculation treatment and no reduction of HCV infectivity within the cells, suggesting the direct effect of bee venom on the inhibition of HCV particle infectivity. Moreover, the authors noticed that the active compound of bee venom is insusceptible to the treatment with 95 °C and the metalloproteinase inhibitor (1, 10‐phenanthroline). The culture supernatant was still capable of suppressing the production of HCV infectious particles. 67

sec.title: Beeswax
sec.p: Beeswax is composed of hydroxy monoesters and linear wax monoesters (35% to 45%), hydrocarbons (12% to 16%), free fatty acids (12% to 14%), esters and diesters of fatty acids (15% to 27%), fatty alcohols (1%), minerals (Ca, Fe, Mn, P, Cu, K, Na, and Zn), vitamins (A, B6, and B1), flavonoids, and residues of propolis and pollen. 53 Beeswax may cause allergic reactions. 68

Hassan et al. 64 measured the antiviral effect of ethanol and acetone white and black (natural) beeswaxes against human adenovirus serotype 7 (Adeno‐7) and Rift Valley fever virus (RVFV). Both viruses were cultured in Vero cells. Table 2 presents the IC50 values that were obtained. The results suggest that black (natural) and white waxes possess antiviral activity towards the DNA (Adeno‐7) and RNA (RVFV) viruses. The analysis of ethanol white wax extract showed an increase in infectivity titer post‐treatment of Adeno‐7 (0.34 log10 mL−1). For infectivity titer post‐treatment, a 0.00 log10 ml−1 decrease was observed in acetone white wax extract, and in ethanol black (natural) wax extract a 0.66 log10 ml−1 ,decrease was recorded, whereas in acetone black (natural) wax extract a 1.66 log10 mL−1 decrease was noted. In the case of RVFV, a decrease in infectivity titer post‐treatment was observed for ethanol white wax extract (0.34 log10 mL−1), acetone white wax extract (0.50 log10mL−1), ethanol black (natural) wax extract (0.50 log10mL−1), and acetone black (natural) wax extract (0.34 log10 mL−1). In the case of post‐interferon (5 ng mL−1) treatment, there was a decrease in virus infectivity; the titer was 1.0 log10 mL−1 for RVFV. 64

sec.title: Honey
sec.p: Honey is composed of sugars (70% to 80%), water, proteins and amino acids, enzymes, organic acids, phenolic compounds (flavonoids: anthocyanidins, chalcones, flavanols, flavones, flavanones, and isoflavones; and non‐flavonoids: phenolic acids), vitamins (B complex and C), and minerals (K, S, Cl, Ca, P, I, Mg, Na, Fe, Cu, Mn, Se, and Zn). 53 , 69 The pH of honey is from 3.2 to 4.5. 70 The antiviral activity of honey is related to the osmotic effect, low pH, and natural compounds such as hydrogen peroxide, phenolic acids, flavonoids (quercetin, rutin, isorhamnetin, quercitrin, and isoquercetin), and lysozyme. 54 Honey may cause adverse effects such as allergies (if consumed in excess or when people are allergic to pollen), diarrhea, or increased levels of glycosylated hemoglobin in the blood (long‐term consumers). The allergy can be caused by propolis. 71 Honey has been called a supersaturated sugar syrup and almost 80% of its total weight is sugar. The high sugar concentration of honey results in lower water activity (aw). The optimum aw values for bacteria, yeast and molds are 0.9, 0.7 and 0.8, respectively. 72

Zeina et al. 73 analyzed the antiviral effect of honey solutions in physiological saline against the rubella virus using an African green monkey kidney (Vero) cell line. Vero cells were incubated for 4 days with honey solutions. The authors observed that honey solutions in all analyzed concentrations (1:1, 1:5, 1:10, 1:100, and 1:1000) killed the virus in infected cells without killing Vero cells. The virus concentration used ranged from 10 to 109 virus/mL, which suggests that the honey solution possesses antiviral activity against the rubella virus. 73

To test the anti‐HSV‐1 activity of honey, Ghapanchi et al. 74 evaluated the antiviral effect of commercial honey, while Hashemipour et al. 75 measured the antiviral effect of manuka honey and acyclovir (from 5 to 800 μg mL−1). HSV‐1 was cultured in Vero cells. 74 , 75 Ghapanchi et al. 74 observed a dose‐dependent increase in viral inhibition. At 0% concentration there were 100 000 plaque‐forming units (PFU) mL−1, after using honey at a concentration of 2.5% their number decreased to 10 000 PFU ml−1, after using honey at the concentration of 5% it decreased to 5 000 PFU ml−1, after using honey at 10% the number lowered to 500 PFU ml−1, after using honey at 20 % it decreased to 25 PFU ml−1 and in the range of honey concentrations of 0 to 30–50% there were 0 PFU ml−1. 74 Hashemipour et al. 75 observed an inhibitory effect towards HSV‐1 after treatment with manuka honey (100, 250, and 500 μg mL−1) and acyclovir (100 μg mL−1) because the number of plaques decreased to zero. Moreover, viral load was also reduced from 70.795 to 43.3 and 0 PFU mL−1 after treatment with honey and acyclovir (100 μg mL−1). 75 This suggests that both commercial and manuka honeys treat HSV‐1 effectively. 74

Shahzad and Cohrs 76 measured the antiviral effect of clover and manuka honey against varicella zoster virus (VZV). Varicella zoster virus was cultured in human malignant melanoma cells (MeWo). Table 2 shows the EC50 values of anti‐VZV activity for clover and manuka honey. The authors suggested that the tested honey possesses significant activity against VZV and could be a readily available, inexpensive, and very effective method for treating zoster rash. 76

To reveal the anti‐influenza activity of honey, Babaei et al. 61 evaluated the antiviral effect of honey (22 g L−1) against avian influenza H9N2 viruses in Japanese quails, and Watanabe et al. (2014) 77 analyzed the antiviral effect of manuka (Leptospermum scoparium), soba (Fagopyrum esculentum; buckwheat), kanro (honeydew), acacia (Robinia pseudoacacia), and renge (Astragalus sinicus) honeys against H1N1. Babaei et al. observed an increase of about 2.0 in H9N2 antibody titrations. 61 H1N1 was cultured in Madin–Darby canine kidney (MDCK) cells. The IC50 and SI values (Table 2) obtained by Watanabe et al. 77 suggest that the honey samples inhibit H1N1 replication. The analysis of plaque inhibition assay showed that manuka honey did not affect the plaque amount compared to the control, since the results were 102.3 ± 1.3% for manuka honey 6.25 mg ml−1 and 110.3 ± 6.4% for manuka honey 25 mg ml −1. It is worth nothing that, treating the virus with manuka honey before infection caused a significant decrease in plaque amount compared to the control, to 13.7 ± 0.8% for manuka honey 6.25 mg ml−1 and 0% for 25 mg ml−1. The results showed the virucidal activity of manuka honey. The treatment of cells with manuka honey during infection caused a decrease in plaque by 51.0 ± 2.7% for the use of 6.25 mg ml−1 of manuka honey and 7.5 ± 4.2% for 25 mg mL−1 of the same honey. Following the treatment of cells with manuka honey after infection, the decrease in plaque was 63.2 ± 17.3% for 6.25 mg ml−1 of manuka honey and 5.6 ± 1.1% for 25 mg mL−1 of the same honey. The authors also observed the time‐dependent virucidal activity of manuka honey. In the case of zanamivir (100 nM), a significant decrease in plaque numbers, that is a decrease by 31.3 ± 1.9% was observed after infection. 77 Thus, it can be concluded that the tested honey samples possess anti‐influenza activity.

Babaei et al. 61 also evaluated the antiviral effect of honey (22 g L−1) against Newcastle disease virus (NDV). The authors observed an increase of about 1.4 in NDV antibody titrations, which shows that honey increased antibody titrations against Newcastle disease virus compared with virginamycin. 61

Behbahani 78 analyzed the antiviral effect of eight monofloral Iranian honeys towards HIV‐1. HIV‐1 was cultured in peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) from five healthy volunteers. Honey was obtained from Petroselinum sativum, Nigella sativa, Citrus sinensis, Zataria multiflora, Citrus aurantium, Zizyphus mauritiana, Chamaemeleum nobile, and Astragalus gummifer flowers. The authors observed a dose‐dependent decrease in viral replication after treatment with honey from C. sinensis, Z. multiflora, C. aurantium, Z. mauritiana, N. sativa, and P. sativum flowers. The effect was not observed in the case of C. nobile and A. gummifer flowers. Table 2 shows the EC50 and SI values that were obtained. The methylglyoxal control had EC50 and SI values of 2.2 μg mL−1 and 590. 78

Kalėdienė et al. 79 evaluated the antiviral effect of Camelyn honey extract towards severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS‐CoV‐2), which was cultured in Vero E6 cells. Camelyn ampoules for injection were made from a selected honey extract and contained 35% Camelyn and 65% water. Analysis of the SARS‐CoV‐2 plaque reduction assay results showed that Camelyn in concentrations from 9.08 to 72.6 μg mL did not significantly reduce viral plaque in case of the cells infected with 100 PFU, because the observed decrease was only from 4.5 to 13.5% At a concentration of 145.3 μg mL−1, Camelyn reduced virus plaques to 53.85%, and the EC50 was calculated to be 192.4 μg mL−1 (Table 2). The use of Camelyn tablets showed a more substantial inhibitory effect because the calculated EC50 value was 116.27 ± 73.39 μg mL−1 (Table 2). When cells were infected with 25–30 PFU, the authors also observed a 30‐33% decrease in viral plaque when the concentrations from 9.08 to 36.3 μg mL−1 were used, and a significant decrease when using the concentration of 72.6 μg mL−1 and higher ones. The EC50 was calculated to be 85.7 μg mL−1 (Table 2). The calculated EC50 values for favipiravir and remdesivir were 15.71 and 0.616 μg mL−1, respectively. All the data suggest that Camelyn inhibits replication of SARS‐CoV‐2 at the initial stage. 79

Ruoff et al. 80 analyzed the impact of honey against norovirus GII.4 and GII.10. The IC50 values against GII.4 and GII.10 presented in Table 2 suggest that all of the honeys possess an antiviral effect against norovirus. Moreover, the authors observed that the analyzed honeys changed the diameter and heterogeneity of the GII.4 and GII.10 virus‐like particles. 80

sec.title: Propolis
sec.p: Propolis, often referred to as ‘bee glue’ is a sticky and resinous substance produced by bees from plant materials, including leaves, flowers, and bud exudates. Bees transform these natural elements using the combination of their secretions and wax. 72 Bee glue is composed of resins (50%), waxes (30%), essential oils (5%), pollen (5%), polyphenols, flavonoids, amino acids, minerals, and vitamins (A, B complex, and E). The antiviral activity of propolis is related to galangin, chrysin, luteolin, apigenin, pinocembrin, kaempferol, quercetin as well as caffeic, benzoic, and p‐coumaric acids. 53 , 54 These compounds can decrease or block viral entrance and/or adsorption into the host cells. 54 Propolis is usually non‐toxic but may cause allergic reactions. 58

El Hady and Hegazi 81 measured the antiviral activity of 70% ethanol east Nile delta propolis extract (from Dakahlia, Ismailia, and Sharkia provinces) towards reovirus (vaccinal strain S 1133). The analyzed viruses were cultured in the primary monolayer cultures of chicken embryo fibroblast (CEF) or ‘inoculated into the allantoic cavity of 9 days old embryonated chicken eggs’ 81 . The values of an embryo‐infected dose of 50 ml (EID50 mL−1) that were obtained were 1.03 × 108 viral particles per ml. The number of reovirus particles was from 1.1 × 105 to 3.3 × 104 after incubation with Dakahlia, Ismailia, and Sharkia propolis in the 1.0 mg mL−1 concentration. East Nile delta propolis therefore decreases the infectivity of the reoviruses. Ismailia propolis showed the most potent activity against the reovirus. 81

Búfalo et al. 82 measured the antiviral effect of Brazilian propolis extracts from Sao Paulo, Minas Gerais, and Parana state against poliovirus type 1 (PV1). PV‐1 was cultured in HEp‐2 cells (human laryngeal epidermoid carcinoma cells). The most effective antiviral action was shown by propolis (10.9%), cinnamic acid (10.5%), and caffeic acid (8.5%). In the case of viral replication inhibition, the results were 52.2, 29.8, and 26.7%, respectively. In the pretreatment, the highest reductions in RNA quantification were observed with caffeic acid (90%) and cinnamic acid (89%) at a concentration of 25 μg 100 μL−1. At concentrations of 5 and 10 μg 100 μL−1, the observed reduction was from 65% to 79%. Propolis (5 and 10 μg 100 μL−1) showed 41% and 60% reductions. The post‐treatment results showed that the most efficient variables were for propolis (39.1%), caffeic acid (22.3%), and cinnamic acid (7.9%). All the results suggest that propolis (10 μg 100 μL−1) is the most effective against PV‐1. 82 Brazilian propolis may therefore be effective in poliovirus treatment.

Zeedan et al. 83 analyzed the antiviral effect of water and ethanol extract of Egyptian propolis against isolated and referenced parapoxviruses (PPV). The analysis of the pock reduction assay showed a decrease in the infectivity titer of both virus strains. Log infectivity titer EID50 values for reference PPV were 5.3 ± 0.130, 2.9 ± 0.218, and 2.5 ± 0.144 for the control, ethanol propolis extract, and water propolis extract. In the case of isolated PPV log infectivity titer, EID50 values were 4.46 ± 0.226, 2.3 ± 0.114, and 2.8 ± 0.123 for the control, ethanol propolis extract, and water propolis extract. 83

Labska et al. 84 analyzed the antiviral effect of the Czech Republic propolis special extract GH 2002 against varicella zoster virus (VZV). Varicella zoster virus was cultured in human embryonic lung fibroblasts (LEP). The pre‐treatment of cells with propolis extract before the infection did not show any effect, whereas the incubation of VZV with propolis extract caused a significant decrease in VZV multiplication. The IC50 value is presented in Table 2. Propolis extract (100 μg mL−1) decreased infectivity by 93.9%. Moreover, adding propolis extract after penetration of VZV into LEP does not significantly reduce plaque formation. 84

Ruoff et al. 80 also analyzed the antiviral effect of propolis against norovirus GII.4 and GII.10. The IC50 values obtained against GII.4 and GII.10 for 96% ethanol propolis extract and DMSO (dimethyl sulfoxide) propolis extract are shown in Table 2. Moreover, the authors observed that the propolis samples increased the heterogeneity of the GII.4 and GII.10 virus‐like particles. 80

Silva‐Beltrán et al. 85 analyzed the antiviral effect of Brazilian green and red propolis extract as well as brown Mexican propolis extract towards human coronavirus 229E (HCoV‐229E). HCoV‐229E was cultured in human lung fibroblast cells (MRC‐5). The authors observed that the most effective was green propolis extract in concentrations of 12.5 and 40 μg mL−1 (infectivity reduction values were from 90% to 99%) and brown propolis extract in concentrations from 6.25 to 25 μg mL−1 (infectivity reduction values were from 80% to 90%). The least effective was red propolis extract, which, in concentrations higher than green and brown propolis extracts, showed infectivity reduction values lower than 70%. The EC50 values obtained for quercetin, caffeic acid, rutin were 77.208 ± 1.23, 127.610 ± 0.99, and 116.640 ± 0.77 μg mL−1, respectively. Table 2 provides EC50 values for brown, green, and red propolis extracts. The therapeutic index values obtained were 3.366 μg mL−1 for quercetin, 2.778 μg mL−1 for caffeic acid, 2.204 μg mL−1 for rutin, 2.597 μg mL−1 for brown propolis extract, 3.259 μg mL−1 for green propolis extract, and 1.902 μg mL−1 for red propolis extract. These values suggest that green propolis extract and quercetin are more effective in HCoV‐229E treatment. 85

Woźniak et al. 86 measured the antiviral effect of Polish propolis extract towards human papillomaviruses (HPV16). HPV16 was cultured in HaCaT cells. The authors observed a reduction of HPV16 infection by 30% following treatment with propolis extract from the Łódzkie province (5 ng μL−1) and by 40% with extract from Lesser Poland at the same concentration. The effect was not observed after treatment with propolis extracts from Pomerania, Greater Poland, and West Pomerania. 86

Vilhelmova‐Ilieva et al. 87 evaluated the antiviral effect of six extracts of Bulgarian propolis against structurally different viruses: human coronavirus strain OC‐43 (HCoV OC‐43), human respiratory syncytial virus type 2 (HRSV‐2) (enveloped RNA viruses), human herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV‐1) (enveloped DNA virus), human rhinovirus type 14 (HRV‐14) (non‐enveloped RNA virus) and human adenovirus type 5 (HadV‐5) (non‐enveloped DNA virus). Table 2 presents the IC50 and SI values that were obtained. The authors analyzed the influence of six propolis extracts on the viability of extracellular virions. The results indicate that enveloped viruses were more sensitive to the effects of propolis extracts. The authors also observed that almost all tested propolis extracts inhibited the adsorption of viruses to the cell, This affected herpes viruses to a greater extent than coronaviruses. When propolis extracts were applied before viral infection, they showed a protective effect on healthy cells. 87

Amoros et al. 88 evaluated the antiviral effect of French propolis against HSV‐1, HSV‐2, acyclovir‐resistant mutant HSV (HSV‐R), adenovirus type 2 (Adeno‐2), poliovirus type 2 (PV), and vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV). All of the viruses were cultured in Vero cells. The authors noticed that 2 h incubation with DMSO only and propolis in concentrations up to 2500 μg mL−1 did not impact PV and Adeno‐2 infectivity. Interestingly, HSV‐1, HSV‐2, and VSV were susceptible – the infectivity was reduced to zero after 2 h incubation with propolis (500 μg mL−1). In the case of HSV‐2, the effect was also observed after 15, 30, and 60 min of incubation with propolis (500 μg mL−1) and 2 h of incubation with propolis (250 μg mL−1). In the case of HSV‐1, the effect was also observed after 30 and 60 min of incubation with propolis (500 μg mL−1). The analysis of plaque formation showed that propolis (30 μg mL−1) inhibited plaque formation of PV, whereas propolis (14 μg mL−1) reduced the number of plaques by 50%. In the case of the other viruses, the reduction in the number of plaques by propolis was not significant. Interestingly, in the case of HSV‐1, HSV‐1 R, HSV‐2, Adeno‐2, and VSV, propolis in the concentration of 10 μg ml−1 reduced the size of plaques (e.g., HSV‐1 and VSV) by 50%, and in the concentration of 30 μg ml−1 by 75% in comparison to the control. Moreover, the analysis of the yield of infectious viruses showed that propolis was the most effective against PV, whereas HSV‐1, HSV‐2, and HSV R were more resistant (viral replication was partially inhibited). 88

Many research groups analyzed the antiviral effect of propolis against HSV. For example Amaros et al. 88 , 89 , Nolkemper et al. 98 , Schnitzler et al. 90 , Shimizu et al. 91 , Sartori et al. 92 , Bankova et al. 93 , Yildirim et al. 94 , Hochheim et al. 95 , Demir et al. 96 , and Sangboonruang et al. 97 Amaros et al. 88 measured the antiviral effect of French propolis on HSV‐1 cultured in Vero cells. The authors obtained the viral titer's reduction factor (log10) by comparison with untreated controls. The study showed that incubation of infected Vero cells with propolis caused a dose‐dependent decrease in viral multiplication – an increase from 1.0 to 3.0 log10 values was observed for propolis in the concentration range from 10 to 30 μg mL−1. At a concentration of 72 μg mL−1, the authors observed 50% cytotoxicity of Vero cells (CC50). The authors also noticed that flavonols were more active than flavones. 88 In 1994, Amoros et al. 89 measured the effect on the virus replication. The researchers evaluated the replication quantitatively using the titer reduction assay after one and a few rounds of multiplication, and they inoculated the cultures at a multiplicity of infection (MOI) of 1 and of 0.001. In the single‐cycle experiment, incubation with propolis at concentrations ranging from 6.25 to 50 μg mL−1 resulted in infectious titers between 2.5 and 3.2 log10. The infectious titer was not observed after incubation with acyclovir in the same concentrations. In the case of multiple cycles, the incubation with propolis (from 6.25 to 50 μg mL−1) and the infectious titer was from 0.75 to 3 log10, respectively. Incubation with acyclovir in the same concentrations resulted in infectious titers between 2 and 3.25 log10. This can suggest that propolis is more effective against HSV‐1 in lower concentrations. The authors also observed an approximately eightfold decrease in viral DNA production following treatment with 15 μg mL−1 of propolis and a 32‐fold decrease with 30 μg mL−1. 89 Thus, the experiments mentioned above suggest that French propolis extract may treat HSV effectively.

In the case of the Czech Republic propolis extract, Nolkemper et al. 98 evaluated the antiviral effect of aqueous and ethanolic Moravian propolis extract against HSV‐2 cultured in RC‐37 cells (African green monkey kidney cells). Table 2 presents the IC50 and SI values for HSV‐2 with aqueous and ethanolic extract. The maximum non‐toxic concentrations for RC‐37 cells were 0.03% for the aqueous extract and 0.001% for the ethanolic extract. The plaque reduction assays showed that propolis extracts in the 0.03 and 0.001% concentrations reduced plaque formation by more than 99%. The authors also observed that 60 min of incubation of cells almost completely abolished viral infectivity. Acyclovir reduced viral replication by 98.8 ± 3.1%, aqueous extract by 22.9 ± 1.6%, and ethanol extract by 6.3 ± 0.7%. In pretreatment of the virus, the results were 10.7 ± 1.8, 99.4 ± 2.7, and 99.6 ± 2.5% for acyclovir, aqueous propolis extract, and ethanol propolis extract. The virion envelope is therefore impaired by propolis extracts or compounds crucial for viral attachment/viral entry are concealed. 98

In 2010, Schnitzler et al. 90 performed a similar experiment using HSV‐1 cultured in RC‐37 cells. The authors also analyzed propolis ingredients such as caffeic acid, p‐coumaric acid, benzoic acid, galangin, pinocembrin, and chrysin. The maximum non‐toxic concentrations for RC‐37 cells were 0.03% for the aqueous extract, 0.001% for the ethanolic extract, 0.003% for caffeic acid, 0.001% for p‐coumaric acid, 0.001% for benzoic acid, 0.0005% for galangin, 0.003% for pinocembrin, and 0.00004% for chrysin. The SIs were 100 for the aqueous extract, 485 for the ethanolic extract, 3.3 for galangin, and 20 for chrysin. The IC50 values for HSV‐1 were 0.0004 and 0.000035% for aqueous and ethanolic extract. 90 Thus, the experiments mentioned above suggest that the Czech Republic ethanol propolis extract may treat HSV effectively.

Shimizu et al. 91 analyzed the antiviral effect of Brazilian propolis ethanol extracts against HSV‐1 in vivo using BALB/c female (6 weeks old, 18–21 g) mice. The authors administrated propolis extracts (10 mg kg−1) orally to HSV‐1 infected mice on days 0 to 6 after infection. HSV‐1 was cultured in Vero E6 cells. Three kinds of propolis extracts were tested: (I) from Baccharis erioclada collected in Rio Grande do Sul State; (II) from Baccharis dracunculifolia collected in Minas Gerais State; and (III) from Myrceugenia euosma collected in Rio Grande do Sul State. Treatment of mice infected by HSV‐1 (2 × 105 PFU/mouse) showed a significant decrease in the development of skin lesions from 3.3 to 6.6 days. 91

Propolis extracts significantly inhibited skin lesions in mice infected with HSV‐1 at a dose of 1 × 106 PFU/mouse, delaying lesion onset from 3.3 to 5 days. These findings suggest that all tested propolis samples reduced the development and progression of HSV‐1‐induced skin lesions. Evaluation of anti‐HSV‐1 activity in mice on day 4 after infection showed that propolis extract II and acyclovir significantly reduced viral titers in both the brain and skin. In the brain, viral titers decreased from 6.1 ± 0.07 log10 PFU/organ in the control group to 5.7 ± 0.09 and 5.4 ± 0.14 log10 PFU/organ following treatment with propolis extract II and acyclovir (5 mg mL−1), respectively. In the skin, titers decreased from 2.2 ± 0.02 log10 PFU/organ in the control to less than 1.0 ± 0.00 log10 PFU/organ after treatment with propolis extracts II and III and acyclovir. The propolis extract I had no significant effect on virus titers in either tissue. 91

The EC50 values for propolis extracts I, II, and III and for acyclovir were 61.0 ± 0.2, 51.4 ± 1.3, >50, and 0.48 ± 0.05 μg mL−1, respectively (Table 2). The corresponding SI values were 1.5 for extract I, 1.6 for extract II, less than 0.9 for extract III, and more than 62.5 for acyclovir, indicating that extracts I and II exhibit anti‐HSV‐1 activity. 91

Analysis of the effect of propolis extracts on delayed‐type hypersensitivity (DTH) reactions showed that only extracts I and III enhanced the DTH response 36 h and/or 48 h after challenge with HSV‐1 antigen, a key immune defense mechanism against intradermal HSV infection. No such effect was observed with extract II. 91

Sartori et al. 92 evaluated the antiviral activity of a brown Brazilian propolis hydroalcoholic extract against HSV‐2 in vivo, using African green monkey kidney (Vero) cells. In female adult BALB/c mice (20–25 g) infected with HSV‐2 (1 × 102 PFU mL−1), the infection caused intense disorganization of dense and loose connective tissue, with marked leukocyte infiltration in the epidermis and dermis. Following treatment with the hydroethanolic extract, inflammation was reduced and no morphological alterations in the dermis were observed. 92

Hochheim et al. 95 assessed the antiviral effects of Brazilian propolis extracts on HSV‐1 cultured in Vero cells. The IC50 and SI values obtained for various extract fractions – ethyl acetate, butanol, dichloromethane FM14, and dichloromethane FM45 – under simultaneous, virucidal, and adsorption inhibition conditions are presented in Table 2. Brazilian propolis extracts demonstrated antiviral activity against HSV‐1 and appear to have been effective during the initial stages of infection, 95 supporting their potential use in HSV treatment.

Bankova et al. 93 measured the antiviral activity of Canadian propolis extract against HSV‐1 and HSV‐2 cultured in Madin–Darby bovine kidney (MDBK) cells. The analysis of HSV‐1 adsorption showed a decrease in viral adsorption if viral inoculation was from 103 to 105 CCID50, the concentration of propolis extract was 0.1 mg mL−1, and the duration of adsorption was 60 min or longer. The incubation of infected cells with propolis extract (3.2 and 10 mg mL−1) showed a significant virucidal effect after 15 min or more prolonged incubation. In the case of propolis extract (1 mg mL−1), the effect was observed only after 3 h of incubation, whereas the virucidal effect was not observed at a concentration of 0.32 mg mL−1. A similar effect was recorded also for HSV‐2. 93

Yildirim et al. 94 measured the antiviral effect of Hatay propolis on HSV‐1 and HSV‐2 cultured in HEp‐2 cells. The authors observed that after using the 100TCID50 dilution from the virus stocks, propolis (25, 50, and 100 μg mL−1) showed similar activity to acyclovir – both compounds inhibited HSV‐1 replication after 24 h. The HSV‐2 propolis showed antiviral activity after 48 h of incubation, and the observed effect was time dependent (it increased during incubation). The authors also noticed a significant decrease in the number of viral DNA copies of HSV‐1 and HSV‐2 in comparison with the control. 94 Demir et al. 96 evaluated the antiviral effect of different propolis extracts (glycol, ethanol, glycerol, and soya oil) on HSV‐1 and HSV‐2 cultured in immortalized human keratinocytes (HaCaT). Table 2 shows the EC50 and SI values that were obtained for HSV‐1 and HSV‐2. The authors noticed that glycolic propolis extract possessed more potent antiviral activity against HSV‐1 and HSV‐2 than acyclovir. Moreover, glycolic, ethanolic, and soya oil propolis extracts were more effective in HSV‐2 treatment than acyclovir. 96 Sangboonruang et al. 97 evaluated the antiviral effect of ethanolic extract of Thailand's propolis nanoparticles against HSV‐2 cultured in Vero cells. The authors observed that propolis nanoparticle extract decreased plaque formation significantly in a concentration‐dependent manner. Table 2 presents the IC50 and SI values that were obtained. The researchers noticed that propolis nanoparticles extracted in a 1.25 mg mL−1 concentration showed a similar effect (IC90) to acyclovir. 97 To summarize, the experiments described above show that the propolis extracts from different geographical regions can potentially be used in HSV‐1 and/or HSV‐2 treatment.

The antiviral effect of propolis against NDV was analyzed by a few research groups: Hegazi et al., 99 Babaei et al., 61 and Alkhalefa et al. 100 Hegazi et al. 99 measured the antiviral effect of propolis towards different lentogenic strains of Newcastle disease virus (NDV): HB1, Lasota, Colon 30, and F‐strain, as well as mesogenic K strain and velogenoic (VV‐NDV). Propolis at a concentration of 3.0 mg/mL decreases the infectivity of lentogenic NDV. The infectivity mean titers were 109.96 and 108.39 for the control and HB1 strain, 109.37 and 106.94 for the control and Lasota strain, 109.20 and 106.58 for the control and Colon 30 strain, as well as 109.73 and 107.74 for the control and F‐strain. The most potent effect was observed against the Lasota and Colon 30 strains. For mesogenic K strain infectivity, the mean titers were 106.74, and 108.58 for the control, whereas for VV‐NDV infectivity, the mean titers were 104.42, and 107.33 for the control. It can be concluded that propolis (3 mg mL−1) reduces the infectivity of lentogenic, mesogenic, and velogenic strains of NDV, and the most potent inhibitory effect was observed towards VV‐NDV. 99 Babaei et al. 61 evaluated the antiviral effect of ethanol propolis extract (1000 and 5000 mg kg−1) against Newcastle disease virus (NDV). The authors observed a 1.7‐fold increase in NDV antibody titrations for ethanol propolis extract 1 (1000 mg kg−1), which demonstrates that propolis extracts increased antibody titrations against Newcastle viruses in comparison with virginamycin, except for propolis extract 1. 61 Alkhalefa et al. 100 analyzed the antiviral effect of Egyptian ethanolic propolis extract on two NDV isolates (MW881875 and MW881876) cultured in Vero cells. The prevention rate after incubation with propolis at a concentration of 13 μg mL or amantadine (150 μg mL) was 25.48 ± 3.56 and 71.84 ± 4.28%, respectively. The EC50 values that were obtained were 78.31 ± 5.17 (Table 2) and 39.86 ± 3.42 μg mL−1, respectively, whereas the SI values were 1.39 and 8.9, respectively. The authors also observed a significant decrease in viral titer. The TCID50 values that were obtained were reduced from 4 log10 in the control samples to 2.66 log10 in the samples with propolis (13 μg mL−1). 100 All results in the experiments mentioned above indicate that propolis extracts have antiviral activity against NDV.

Many research groups analyzed the antiviral effect of propolis against influenza viruses: Kujumgiev et al. 101 , Shimizu et al. 102 , Urushisaki et al. 103 , Takemura et al. 104 , Babaei et al. 61 , and Governa et al. 105 . Kujumgiev et al. 101 evaluated the antiviral effect of propolis 70% ethanol extracts from different regions (Albania, Brazil, Bulgaria, Canary Islands, Egypt, and Mongolia) against avian influenza virus (H7N7). The virus was cultured in 11‐day‐old fertile hens' eggs and allantoic fluid. Table 2 presents the significant selectivity index (SI) values, calculated as TC50/EC50 ratios, for samples from Bulgaria, Mongolia, Albania, and Brazil. The Brazilian samples include those from Parana, Limera, and Piani (produced by Melipona compressipes), as well as from Parana (produced by Melipona quadrifasciata anthidioides). Propolis (0.1%) from the Piani state had the most potent effect. 101 Babaei et al. 61 evaluated the antiviral effect of ethanol propolis extract (1000 and 5000 mg kg−1) against avian influenza H9N2 viruses in Japanese quails. The authors observed a 1.75‐ and 2.1‐ fold increase for propolis extracts 1 and 2. Consequently, propolis extracts increased antibody titrations against avian influenza H9N2 viruses in comparison with virginamycin, except for propolis extract 1 and H9N2, for which a decrease in viral titer was observed. 61 In the case of the influenza A virus (H1N1) cultured in MDCK cells, Shimizu et al. 102 measured the antiviral effect of 13 South Brazilian propolis ethanol extracts (AF‐05, AF‐06, AF‐07, AF‐08, AF‐17, AF‐18, AF‐19, AF‐20, AF‐M1, AF‐M2, AF‐M3, AF‐G1, and AF‐G12). Table 2 presents the EC50 values that were obtained. The EC50 for ribavirin (the positive control) was 20.2 ± 11.7 μg mL−1. Only four extracts (AF‐08, AF‐17, AF‐19, and AF‐M1) proved possible anti‐influenza virus activity, as EC50 values were lower than cytotoxic concentration for MDCK cells. The in vivo study using female DBA/2 Cr mice (6 weeks old, 17–19 g) infected with 1600 PFU of H1N1 or phosphate‐buffered saline (PBS) showed that only AF‐08 may be effective in H1N1 treatment without toxicity (‘did not produce significant body weight loss in uninfected mice’ 102 for 11 days). The infected mice treated by AF‐08 at 0.4, 2, or 10 mg kg−1 ‘were still alive on day ten after infection’ 102 . It is worth noting that AF‐08 (2 and 10 mg kg−1) significantly prolonged the survival time of H1N1 infected mice for 8.3 ± 0.7 and 9.3 ± 0.5 days, respectively, in comparison with the control (6.1 ± 0.6 days), which suggests that AF‐08 decreases H1N1 infection in a dose‐dependent manner. Moreover, AF‐08 (10 mg kg−1) reduced viral yields in the bronchoalveolar lavage fluid of infected mouse lungs as effectively as oseltamivir (1 mg kg−1). 102 Urushisaki et al. 103 analyzed the antiviral effect of Brazilian green propolis water extract. The EC50 values that were obtained for propolis water extract, chlorogenic acid, caffeic acid, 3,5‐dicaffeoylquinic acid, 3,4‐dicaffeoylquinic acid, 4,5‐dicaffeoylquinic acid, 3,4,5‐tricaffeoylquinic acid, and quinic acid were 183.1 ± 6.0 (Table 2), 341.5, 191.2, 207.8, 81.1 ± 2.9, 280.6, 114.6, and >1561 μM, respectively. 3,4‐Dicaffeoylquinic acid is therefore the most effective against H1N1. 103

Takemura et al. 104 analyzed the antiviral effect of the main compound of Brazilian propolis (3,4‐dicaffeoylquinic acid) in vivo. Six‐week‐old female BALB/c mice were infected with 5.1 × 108 PFU of H1N1. The authors observed a significant decrease in body weight from 0 to 7 dpi (in the control group), no effect on phenotype (in propolis water extract, propolis ethanol extract, and chlorogenic acid group) as well as inhibition of body weight loss (in 3,4‐dicaffeoylquinic acid and oseltamivir groups). Moreover, treatment of infected mice with 3,4‐dicaffeoylquinic acid and oseltamivir did not affect tumor necrosis factor‐related apoptosis‐inducing ligand (TRAIL) mRNA expression (at 4 dpi) or an increase in TRAIL expression after 3,4‐dicaffeoylquinic acid treatment (at 7 dpi). This indicates that ‘oseltamivir treatment decreased IAV HA mRNA expression without the effect on TRAIL mRNA expression, while 3,4‐dicaffeoylquinic acid treatment moderately decreased IAV HA mRNA expression and increased TRAIL mRNA expression with a delay’. 104

Governa et al. 105 measured the antiviral effect of Italian poplar propolis. The pre‐ and post‐adsorption of H1N1 showed that propolis did not reduce viral load in concentrations below 25 mg mL−1. The IC50 values that were obtained for propolis was 35.29 ± 4.08 μg mL−1 and for oseltamivir it was 5.88 ± 0.89 μg mL−1 (Table 2). The data showed that propolis was effective against H1N1 in cytotoxic concentrations in the MDCK cells. 105 The results mentioned above suggest that propolis extracts from different geographical regions may help treat different strains of influenza viruses (H1N1, H7N7, or H9N2).

The antiviral effect of propolis against HIV was analyzed by two research groups: Ito et al. 106 and Gekker et al. 107 Ito et al. 106 analyzed the antiviral effect of moronic acid derivatives and the melliferone‐related triterpenoid isolated from Brazilian propolis on HIV‐1 virus cultured in the H9 cell line. Azidothymidine was used as a control. The analysis of viral replication showed that EC50 values were <0.1 μg mL−1 for moronic acid, 0.22 μg mL−1 for betulonic acid, 2.19 μg mL−1 for 3‐(3,4‐dimethoxyphenyl)‐2‐propenal, 2.70 μg mL−1 for 3α‐hydroxy‐3‐deoxymoronic acid, 1.0 μg mL−1 for 3‐O‐(3′,3′‐dimethylsuccinyl) moronic acid, and 0.00289 μg mL−1 for azidothymidine. The therapeutic index values obtained were >186 for moronic acid, 8 for betulonic acid, 8.62 for 3‐(3,4‐dimethoxyphenyl)‐2‐propenal, 8.17 for 3α‐hydroxy‐3‐deoxymoronic acid, 18.0 for 3‐O‐(3′,3′‐dimethylsuccinyl) moronic acid, and 173 000 for azidothymidine. The results suggest that moronic acid isolated from Brazilian propolis is most efficient against HIV‐1. 106 Gekker et al. 107 measured the antiviral effect of American, Brazilian (Rio Grande do Sul, Rio de Janeiro, and Minas Gerais), and Chinese propolis (0.8, 2.5, and 66 μg mL−1) ethanol extracts against HIV‐1AT (T‐tropic (X4) strain). HIV‐1AT was cultured in activated CD4+ lymphocyte cultures. The US propolis was obtained from commercial sources in Minnesota (Cannon Bee, Southeast, and Northern), and from three specific locations in Minnesota (Houston, St Paul, and Duluth). In the controls, the p24 antigen level in HIV‐1AT infected cells was about 8 ng mL−1 for propolis of specific locations, while 11 ng mL−1 for propolis from commercial sources, Brazilian and Chinese propolis. The authors noticed a dose‐dependent decrease in the p24 antigen from 8 to 0.5 ng mL−1 in Cannon Bee, 8 to 1 ng mL−1 in Southeast propolis, 9 to 0.5 ng mL−1 in Northern and Chinese propolis extract, 8 to 3 ng mL−1 in Rio Grande do Sul, 8 to 6 ng mL−1 in Rio de Janeiro, 6 to 3 ng mL−1 in Minas Gerais, and 7 to 0.5 ng mL−1 in Houston, St Paul, and Duluth propolis, which suggests that all tested propolis extracts possess potent antiviral activity against HIV. Brazilian propolis extracts were less effective. Furthermore, a cell fusion assay showed that Cannon Honey propolis (22.2 μg mL−1) suppressed cell fusion by 50%, suggesting that the antiviral effect may be caused by inhibiting viral entry into cells. 107 Thus, the results mentioned above indicate that propolis may be effective in HIV treatment.

sec.title: Royal jelly
sec.p: Royal jelly is composed of water (60% to 70%), sugar (12% to 15%), proteins (12%), lipids (5% to 6%), vitamins, and mineral salts, and its pH is from 3.6 to 4.2 54 or between 3.1 and 3.9. 53 Royal jelly peptides or jelleines (jelleine I–IV) possess antiviral activity. 54 The mechanism of antiviral activity may also be related to the impact of 10‐HAD (10‐hydroxy‐2‐decenoic acid), which stimulates white blood cells. Stimulating white blood cells can increase their adhesion to the viruses and cause the destruction of the viruses. 108 Royal jelly may also contain contaminants (pesticides or chloramphenicol). Major royal jelly proteins (MRJP‐1 and MRJP‐2) are significant allergens. 58 Common side effects observed after the use of royal jelly are itching, irritation, or rash. 109

Hashemipour et al. 75 analyzed the impact of Iranian royal jelly against HSV‐1, besides honey's antiviral effect. The authors observed an inhibitory effect towards HSV‐1 after royal jelly (250 μg mL−1) treatment. Moreover, a decrease in viral load was observed from 70,795 to 30 PFU mL−1. The results suggest that royal jelly possesses antiviral activity against HSV‐1. 75

Babaei et al. 61 evaluated the antiviral effect of royal jelly (100 mg/kg) against Newcastle disease virus (NDV) and avian influenza H9N2 viruses in Japanese quails. The authors observed 1.1‐ and 1.9‐fold increases in NDV and H9N2 antibody titrations for royal jelly, which shows that royal jelly increased antibody titrations against H9N2 and NDV in comparison with virginamycin. 61

sec.title: COMPARISON OF ANTIVIRAL PROPERTIES OF BEE PRODUCTS
sec.p: With regard to the values in Table 2, Fig. 3(A)–(C) depicts the mean values of EC50 and IC50 presented in μg mL and SI. To avoid drawing conclusions based on the results from just one experiment, only bee products and viruses with two or more experiment results were analyzed.

caption.p: Antiviral activity of bee products. (A) The graph shows mean EC50 values ± SEM for honey and propolis expressed in μg mL−1 for different types of viruses. Only experiments in which the EC50 value was determined in μg mL−1 were analyzed. 77 , 78 , 84 , 90 , 95 , 101 , 102 (B) The graph shows mean IC50 values ± SEM for bee bread, bee pollen, beeswax, honey, and propolis expressed in μg mL−1 for different types of viruses. Only experiments in which the IC50 value was determined in μg mL−1 were analyzed. 59 , 61 , 64 , 76 , 86 , 94 , 96 (C) The graph shows mean SI values ± SEM for bee bread, bee pollen, honey, and propolis for different types of viruses. Only experiments in which the SI value was determined were analyzed. 59 , 61 , 69 , 76 , 86 , 89 , 90 , 94 , 95 , 96 , 97 , 100

sec.p: The analysis of EC50 values (Fig. 3(A)) show that propolis is the most effective against HCoV and IAV and honey against HIV. Antiviral activity of honey against HCoV and propolis against HSV is lower than their activity against other viruses.

As long as IC50 values are concerned (Fig. 3(B)), beeswax showed strong activity against ADV and RVFV. Interestingly, bee bread is more effective in treating EV and IAV than bee pollen because average IC50 values were 574.6 and 590 μg mL−1, as well as 673.8 and 2884.2 μg mL−1, respectively. Strong antiviral activity against HSV is observed for propolis. Furthermore, honey samples showed the weakest antiviral activity against IAV with the IC50 value of 8100 μg mL−1.

Regarding SI values (Fig. 3(C)), propolis and honey showed similar weak antiviral activity against the influenza virus. Strong antiviral activity was observed in the cases of propolis and HSV, as well as honey and HIV. The analysis showed potent antiviral activity against EV and IAV of bee bread and bee pollen as the SI values that were obtained were 20.6 and 21.5, as well as 145.3 and 28.2, respectively.

Differences in origin, composition, the content of active substances, storage conditions, methods of analysis, and the type of solvent used may have caused the observed differences in EC50, IC50, and SI values. Thus, the standardization of bee products is crucial, as suggested in previous publications. 70 , 110

sec.title: CONCLUSION
sec.p: This review shows that bee products such as bee bread, bee pollen, bee venom, beeswax, honey, propolis, and royal jelly have strong potential for the treatment of viral infections caused by RNA and DNA viruses. Activity has been reported against enteroviruses EV‐68 and EV‐71, Adeno‐7, RVFV, H1N1, H7N7, VSV, RSV, HSV, H3, HCV, VZV, HIV‐1, SARS‐CoV‐2, GII.4, GII.10, NDV, and HCoV‐229E. Analysis indicates that bee products reduce IC50 and EC50 values relative to controls. Their antiviral effects include decreased viral load, inhibition of viral replication, reduced viral DNA synthesis, and impaired viral adsorption to host cells. These products increase SI values and antibody titers against tested viruses, suggesting potential enhancement of humoral immunity (Fig. 4). The mechanisms underlying these antiviral effects vary depending on the bee product type and the specific virus.

caption.p: The mechanisms of bee products' antiviral effects based on the reviewed literature.

sec.p: As in the case of antibacterial activity, standardization of bee products is a crucial problem since their activity depends on their chemical composition, the concentration of active compounds, and the product's origin. Thus, more in vitro and in vivo studies should be performed to confirm the use of bee products as a safe and promising alternative to the drugs used today in antiviral therapy or to support pharmacological treatment.
